sections.skill: Calculate cost of attendance and net price, and compare colleges by what a family will actually pay

questions.prompt: College A lists tuition $14,000, housing and food $13,000, books $1,200, transportation $1,800, and personal costs $2,000. What is the cost of attendance?
questions.intro: Cost of attendance (COA) is a college's estimate of a full year: tuition and fees, housing and food, books and supplies, transportation, and personal expenses.
questions.topic: Cost of attendance and net price
sources: U.S. Department of Education (College Navigator / net price calculators): Colleges must post a net price calculator that estimates cost of attendance minus grants and scholarships. (https://nces.ed.gov/collegenavigator/)

questions.prompt: College A's COA is $32,000. Kira receives a $9,000 grant and a $3,000 scholarship. What is her net price?
questions.intro: Net price = cost of attendance − grants and scholarships (gift aid, which does not have to be repaid). Loans are not subtracted, because they must be paid back.
questions.topic: Cost of attendance and net price
sources: U.S. Department of Education (College Navigator / net price calculators): Colleges must post a net price calculator that estimates cost of attendance minus grants and scholarships. (https://nces.ed.gov/collegenavigator/)

questions.prompt: College B's award lists COA $45,000; grants $22,000; work-study $2,500; loans $5,500. What is the net price?
questions.intro: Award letters mix gift aid with "self-help" aid: work-study (money you earn at a job) and loans (money you repay). Only gift aid lowers the net price.
questions.feedback: $45,000 − $22,000 = $23,000. Work-study must be earned and loans must be repaid.
questions.topic: Cost of attendance and net price

misconceptions.B: Subtracts work-study as if it were a grant
